> **The research decision.** For every number, dataset, and source your project
> leans on, decide whether it is solid enough to build on. You make that call
> twice: once on where the value came from and whose hands it passed through, its
> provenance, and once on whether it was produced well enough, under the right
> definition, for the specific use you have in mind, its quality.

## Why this decision matters

**The decision on the table: whether a number you did not produce yourself is
solid enough to carry your project's weight.**

Picture an advisor, the researcher who will eventually sign off on your project,
reading the first draft of your background section:

> *"You wrote that turnout in this county was 72 percent. Where did that come from?
> Not which website you copied it off. Who counted the ballots, and 72 percent of
> what? Of registered voters, of adults, of adults actually eligible to vote? Bring
> me the office that certified the count, or take the number out."*

A value with no traceable origin is a rumor with a decimal point. Precision is not
the same as trust. This chapter trains you to stop treating a number or a citation
as true because it arrived looking tidy, and to ask two questions of everything you
borrow: where did it come from, and is it any good for what I need it for.

## The concept

**Data provenance** is the documented origin of a value and every hand it passed
through before it reached you [@lebo2013provo] [@wilkinson2016fair]. Example: a turnout figure in a news story, traced
back through a state summary table to the county election office that certified the
count.

That chain has two kinds of links. A **primary source** is the original record
where a value was first produced. Example: the county's certified canvass, the
official document reporting the final vote totals. A **secondary source**
re-reports a value it did not produce. Example: a newspaper table, an encyclopedia
entry, or a data aggregator that copies the county's number. A value is only as
trustworthy as the primary source at the end of its chain.

![Provenance is the origin of a value and every hand it passed through before it reached you. Tracing back to the primary source is your job, not the
tool's.](../images/concepts/provenance_chain.png){fig-alt="Four boxes in a chain. The primary source, the original record where the value was first
produced, drawn with a heavy rule. Then two secondary sources, each re-reporting a value it did not produce. Then the value as it appears in your
file. An arrow curves back from your file to the primary source, labelled trace it back yourself. Below, two boxes name what you must be able to
answer: provenance, where did this value come from and through whose hands; and data quality, whether it is fit for your own question."}

**Data quality** is whether a value is fit for *your* specific use: real, produced
by a method you can name, and defined the way your question needs [@wang1996beyond]. Example: a
turnout rate computed over registered voters is high quality for a question about
whether registered people showed up, and the wrong number for a question about how
much of the adult population takes part. A **mischaracterized value** is a real
number attached to the wrong definition or method. Example: a survey's
self-reported turnout presented as an official count, or a registered-voter rate
cited as though it covered everyone eligible.

Whole datasets carry the same two questions, column by column. Who produced this
variable, who cleaned it, what did they drop, and does the definition behind the
column match the one in your question? A file that lands in your folder with no
answers to those questions is not yet data. It is a rumor in a spreadsheet.

You settle all of it with one habit, the **retrieval-verification loop**: **Ask** a
tool to surface a value and its source, **Retrieve** the primary source yourself,
**Verify** that it exists and reports that value under that definition, and
**Document** where you found it. A citation you have not opened is a lead, not a
source, however confident the tool that handed it to you.

## A worked example

Suppose you are studying whether a local election reform changed participation, and
you need one number to anchor your background section: turnout in a particular
county in a recent presidential election. You ask an AI assistant and get an answer
in about a second. Seventy-two percent, with a source that looks entirely real.

You run the loop instead of copying the number. First, **provenance**. You search
the exact title of the source. If it resolves nowhere, the value is orphaned and
you drop it. If the page is real, you ask whether it *produced* that number or
merely republished it. That question usually sends you one link further back, to
the state's official results summary, and behind that to the county clerk's
certified canvass, which is where the totals were actually settled.

Then, **quality**. You open the canvass and read what the percentage is *of*. Is
the denominator registered voters, all adults, or adults eligible to vote, which
excludes noncitizens and, in some states, people with certain felony convictions?
Those three denominators produce three different turnout numbers for the same
election, and the gaps between them are not small. You also ask whether the figure
was *counted* or *estimated*. Ballots cast are counted. Eligible-population
denominators are estimated from census data. Survey turnout is self-reported, and
people reliably overstate whether they voted, so it is a third kind of number
again.

You cross-check against an independent source that documents its own methods. Two
worth knowing: the United States Elections Project, which publishes
voting-eligible-population turnout estimates and explains exactly how it builds the
denominator, and the Census Bureau's Current Population Survey Voting and
Registration Supplement, which reports self-reported turnout from a large national
survey. When the certified canvass and an independent reference agree on both the
count and the definition, the number has earned a place in your project. When they
disagree, the disagreement *is* the finding. You report both, name the definition
behind each, and say which one your question needs and why.

That a value's usefulness depends on its documented origin and on fitness for the specific use, not on precision alone, is the standard framing of data quality [@wang1996beyond].

The block below is not a simulation. It is the same numerator divided by the three denominators a real turnout figure might be resting on, so you can see how much of the answer the label decides.

```python
import pandas as pd
SEED = 464   # no random draw here: provenance is a chain, not a sample

# One county, one election, three denominators — each a real kind of published
# figure, each answering a different question. Replace these with the numbers
# you retrieve from the canvass and the census table you name.
ballots_cast = 214_318
denominators = {
    "registered voters (clerk's canvass)": 297_664,
    "voting-age population (census estimate)": 341_902,
    "voting-eligible population (estimate)": 312_540,
}
rows = [{"denominator": k, "count": v,
         "turnout %": round(ballots_cast / v * 100, 1)}
        for k, v in denominators.items()]
print(pd.DataFrame(rows).to_string(index=False))
print(f"\nspread across the three : "
      f"{max(r['turnout %'] for r in rows) - min(r['turnout %'] for r in rows):.1f} "
      f"percentage points")
print("one election, one numerator, three published turnout numbers.")
print("a figure with no stated denominator is not yet evidence")
```

## Missing data: the rows you do not see

Suppose the county's election office also mails a short follow-up survey to 4,000
registered voters, drawn at random from its list, asking whether they voted. About
six in ten send it back. Your file has 4,000 rows, but the turnout column is blank
in roughly 1,600 of them. Every summary you compute from that file quietly describes
the people who answered, unless you decide otherwise and say how.

**Missing data** are values that should exist in your file but do not. Example: a
respondent who skipped the income question, a field sensor that failed for a week,
or a firm that never filed one quarter's report. Ask of every blank what you ask of
every value: who dropped it, and why. The answer decides what you can claim.

Researchers sort those reasons into three mechanisms, a classification that goes back
to Rubin [@rubin1976inference] and that later textbooks built into everyday practice
[@little2019statistical; @vanbuuren2018flexible].

- **Missing completely at random** means the chance a value is missing has nothing
  to do with anything, measured or not. Example: a lab technician drops one tray of
  samples picked by accident. You lose precision, but the answer does not tilt.
- **Missing at random** means the chance a value is missing depends only on things
  you did observe. Example: younger voters return the survey less often, and the
  voter file tells you everyone's age. You then assume that, within an age group,
  the people who answered vote like the people who did not.
- **Missing not at random** means the chance a value is missing depends on the
  missing value itself. Example: people who stayed home on election day are less
  likely to return a survey about voting. No column in your file measures that gap.

**Complete-case analysis** means computing your result only from the rows with no
blanks. Example: averaging a column by skipping its empty cells, as most software
does by default. When values are missing completely at random it gives an unbiased
answer, only a less precise one. Under the other two mechanisms it can tilt the
answer, though not always: if the blanks in an outcome depend only on the
explanatory variables in a regression, the slopes fitted to the complete rows can
still be right [@little2019statistical]. A plain average of the outcome, like
county turnout, has no such protection.

Your first move is descriptive. A **missingness table** is the share of blank values
broken down by groups you can observe. Example: 74 percent of older voters answered
and 46 percent of younger voters did. The table cannot reveal whether the
non-answerers differ in the value you care about. It does show the blanks are spread
far more unevenly than chance would produce, so the first mechanism is not your
situation.

**Imputation** means filling each blank with a value predicted from what you did
observe. Example: give each non-answerer the turnout rate of answerers in the same
age group. It removes the whole tilt only when the values are missing at random
given the variables it uses and the model that fills them includes every variable
your later analysis will use. Short of that, it can repair the part of the tilt that
runs through variables you measured and leaves the rest in place.
**Multiple imputation** fills each blank several times with plausible values and
combines the results. Example: twenty filled-in copies of the survey file, analysed
one by one and pooled. It carries the uncertainty of the guess into your interval
[@vanbuuren2018flexible]. No method recovers information your file never held: if
the values are missing not at random, the filled-in values inherit the tilt. And a
single fill, like the one in the example, treated as real data makes your interval
narrower than your knowledge, because the file now pretends the guesses were
observed.

So you add a check that needs no assumption about the blanks. **Bounds** are the
lowest and highest values your answer could take under the most extreme
possibilities for the missing rows, which you can compute whenever the value has
natural limits, like a yes-or-no vote. Example: turnout if every non-answerer stayed
home, and turnout if every one of them voted [@manski1989anatomy]. Bounds are often
wide, and that width is exactly what your missing rows cost you.

The block below builds a constructed county where you can see the true turnout,
something you never get in practice. Answering depends on age, which the file
records, and on voting itself, which it does not.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# 4,000 registered voters drawn at random from one county's list.
# Older people vote more often.
n = 4_000
older = rng.random(n) < 0.5
voted = rng.random(n) < np.where(older, 0.75, 0.50)
# Who answers the follow-up survey? Older people answer more, AND people
# who voted answer more than people who did not: the missing value itself.
answered = rng.random(n) < 0.35 + 0.20 * older + 0.25 * voted

df = pd.DataFrame({"group": np.where(older, "older", "younger"),
                   "voted": voted, "answered": answered})
print(df.groupby("group")["answered"].agg(people="size", share_answered="mean").round(2))

seen = df[df.answered]
missing = (~df.answered).sum()
complete_case = seen.voted.mean()
# Fill each blank with the turnout of answerers in the same age group.
rate = seen.groupby("group").voted.mean()
filled = df.voted.where(df.answered, df.group.map(rate)).mean()
low = seen.voted.sum() / n                 # every non-answerer stayed home
high = (seen.voted.sum() + missing) / n    # every non-answerer voted

print(f"\nshare of rows missing                 : {missing / n:.3f}")
se = np.sqrt(complete_case * (1 - complete_case) / len(seen))
print(f"complete-case turnout                 : {complete_case:.3f}"
      f"  (95% interval {complete_case - 1.96 * se:.3f} to {complete_case + 1.96 * se:.3f})")
print(f"filled in by age group                : {filled:.3f}")
print(f"bounds with no assumption at all      : [{low:.3f}, {high:.3f}]")
print(f"true turnout of all 4,000 (unseen)    : {df.voted.mean():.3f}")
print("\nfilling in by age repairs the age part of the gap, not the voting part;")
print("only the bounds hold whatever the non-answerers did")
```

Read the output against the true value of 62.4 percent. With 40.2 percent of the
rows blank, the complete-case turnout is 73.9 percent, and its 95 percent interval,
72.2 to 75.7, misses the truth: that interval measures sampling noise among the
people who answered, not who stayed silent. Filling in by age group moves it to 71.9
percent, about two points repaired and 9.5 points still wrong, because the rest of
the tilt runs through voting itself. The bounds run from 44.2 to 84.4 percent, a
width of 40 points that equals the share of missing rows. They contain the truth,
and they would contain it whatever the non-answerers did.

Your estimand is turnout among all registered voters in the county, not among the
people who returned the form. The random draw gives you the sampling license from
4,000 voters to the county, but nonresponse breaks it unless you defend an
assumption about why rows went missing, and nothing in the file can confirm that
assumption. The bounds cover only the blanks among the 4,000; carried to the county,
each end also needs a sampling interval. So you report a filled-in estimate, from
multiple imputation so its interval carries the guess, with its assumption written
beside it, the bounds as a sensitivity check, and one outside
benchmark. In a real county the certified canvass counts the ballots, and a survey
figure far above it warns you about who answered and about people overstating that
they voted. When the blanks are outcomes in an experiment, the same logic returns as
attrition on the experimental-causal pathway.

An AI tool writes the missingness table, the imputation code, and the bounds in
seconds. Two habits keep it honest. Ask it to print the number of rows before and
after every step, because code tools often drop incomplete rows or fill blanks with
a column average without telling you, a **silent scope change** from all 4,000
voters to the ones who answered. And treat any sentence like "the data are missing
at random" as your claim to defend, since it is a statement about people you never
heard from. When values go missing or come back false because the question is
sensitive, you can sometimes redesign the question instead: the [survey
experiments](../part7-further-routes/survey-experiments.qmd) route shows how a list
experiment lets people answer without revealing their own answer.

## An AI failure case

You ask for county turnout and the tool returns "72 percent," with a citation to a
real state elections page. Seven details look right, so it is tempting to paste it
straight in. You open the page instead, and the table header reads *percent of
registered voters*, not percent of everyone eligible. The number is real. The
denominator is the wrong one for your question, and the tool swapped it silently.
You catch it two ways. You had written your own expectation first, so a figure that
sits well above what you knew about participation in that county already looked
suspect. Then you read the actual column header rather than the tool's summary of
it, and the mismatch is plain. The value goes into your notes as a
registered-voter rate, and your original question stays open.

*Your pathway is declared and your contract remains provisional; your measurements come next. Before either can be
trusted, this step pins down where your data actually came from.*

The hands-on half of this section lives in the chapter's **companion notebook**: open it in Colab with the badge at the top, and work the steps there.

Each prompt is **commit-first**: write down the value or source you already believe,
then let the tool disagree with something of yours. Treat every one as the start of
a loop rather than a single request. The first answer gives you leads; your second
message names the lead that did not survive retrieval and asks again. Tools that
run the search loop on their own will hand you a longer, tidier list of sources.
Longer and tidier does not mean opened, and opening them is still your job.

::: {.callout-important title="Do not delegate"}
Three calls stay yours. **Whether a value counts as verified** is settled by a source
you opened, not by the tool's confidence. **Whether its definition fits your use** is
a judgment about your specific question, and no lookup makes it for you. And **how
much uncertainty you report** when your sources disagree is yours to state and
defend, because your name goes on the claim the number supports.
:::

1. List every dataset, table, and borrowed number your project uses. Include the
   ones a collaborator handed you and the ones you downloaded months ago and
   stopped thinking about.
2. For each, write four things: who produced it, when, from what original record,
   and every hand it passed through on the way to you. Where a link in that chain
   is missing, write "unknown" instead of guessing. Unknown is a finding.

   **Turn borrowed numbers into a provenance table (delegable).**

   ```text
   Here are five numbers my project borrows: [paste them]. For each, return a row with
   the value, its exact definition (which population, which time window, which
   denominator), the primary source, and whether the value was counted, estimated, or
   self-reported. Return it as a table so I can audit each row on its own.
   ```

   After running, verify (counters *silent scope change*): read each row's definition
   against the definition your question actually needs; a number built on a different
   population can be handed to you as if it were yours.
3. Open the primary source behind the entry your headline claim leans on hardest.
   Read the line that reports the value and the line that defines it, not a summary
   of either.

   **Locate the primary source (delegable).**

   ```text
   Act as a research-data assistant. I have this figure: [paste the value, the place,
   the year, and how it is expressed]. Name the primary source that FIRST reported it,
   with the issuing body, the exact document title, the year, and the definition used,
   including what the denominator is. Only list sources you are confident exist, mark
   anything uncertain, and say for each whether it is the original record or a
   re-report.
   ```

   After running, verify (counters *confident fabrication*): open every source yourself
   before you trust it; a source you cannot retrieve is invented until it opens.
4. Beside each entry, write its definition in your own words and mark whether it
   matches the definition your question needs. Anything marked "no" gets dropped or
   gets reported with the mismatch stated out loud.

   **Red-team the number you like (delegable).**

   ```text
   I plan to build on this figure: [paste value and source]. Act as a hostile reviewer
   and argue it is unreliable for a claim about [your population and time window]:
   wrong denominator, self-reported rather than counted, or copied through a chain of
   summaries. Do not reassure me.
   ```

   After running, verify (counters *sycophantic agreement*): if the reviewer only praises
   your number, push back, then take its strongest objection to the primary source or to
   someone who knows the data better than you do rather than trusting easy approval.
5. Save the record as a file that travels with your project, and note the date you
   retrieved each source. Sources get revised, and a retrieval date is what lets a
   reader tell whether they are looking at your version.
6. Close with the studio's governance trio: write and date your acquisition
   route, update where the data live and who can open them, and recheck the
   permission status against the data as they actually arrived.
7. Log the step in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one entry with a
   named method from the [Verification Guide](../verification-guide.qmd).
   Primary-source reading is the method this chapter is built on, and any borrowed
